title: Choose the database from the access pattern

sections.heading: Relational transactions
sections.text: RDS and Aurora serve relational models and SQL workloads. Select engine compatibility, transaction needs and recovery objectives before choosing an instance.

sections.heading: Key-based operations
sections.text: DynamoDB fits known key-based access patterns. Design keys and indexes from queries; a flexible item schema does not create arbitrary relational joins.

sections.heading: Specialized access
sections.text: OpenSearch serves indexed search, DocumentDB compatible document APIs, and time-series engines time-based analysis. A cache accelerates a path without replacing every source-of-truth requirement.

remember: Choose semantics before scale claims.

title: RDS manages the platform while you own the database design

sections.heading: Select a supported engine
sections.text: RDS offers supported PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2 configurations. Engine, version, edition and licensing affect features.

sections.heading: Delegate platform work
sections.text: Managed provisioning, patching, backups and monitoring reduce administration. You still own schema, indexes, query design, permissions and capacity decisions.

sections.heading: Scale deliberately
sections.text: Storage autoscaling can grow eligible storage within configured limits. It does not solve every CPU, connection or query bottleneck, and does not imply automatic storage shrink.

remember: Managed infrastructure still needs database engineering.

title: An RDS connection needs network and database permission

sections.heading: Prepare the private path
sections.text: Place databases in an appropriate DB subnet group. Validate routes, DNS, security groups and the engine port from the actual application environment.

sections.heading: Keep Lambda connected
sections.text: A function needs a supported private network path to a private database or proxy. Merely granting IAM permission does not create that path.

sections.heading: Separate access gates
sections.text: TLS protects transport; database authentication identifies the user; database grants authorize SQL operations. Test the complete connection, not only a reachable port.

remember: Reachability, authentication and SQL authorization are separate gates.

title: Backups preserve recovery history; replicas serve another purpose

sections.heading: Use automated recovery
sections.text: Automated backups and transaction logs support point-in-time recovery within the retained window. Confirm the latest restorable time and retention settings.

sections.heading: Retain deliberate snapshots
sections.text: Manual snapshots remain until deleted and can support eligible cross-account or cross-Region copies. Encrypted copies also depend on usable KMS keys.

sections.heading: Restore into a new resource
sections.text: A successful backup is not a tested restore. Validate data, security settings, endpoints and application cutover on the restored database.

remember: Recovery succeeds when the application can use the restored data.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas protect different requirements

sections.heading: Protect the writer
sections.text: A classic Multi-AZ DB instance synchronously replicates to a standby in another AZ. The standby supports failover and does not serve ordinary application reads.

sections.heading: Scale reads
sections.text: Read replicas receive asynchronous changes and can serve read traffic. Replication lag matters; eligible cross-Region replicas can support regional recovery.

sections.heading: Plan client recovery
sections.text: Failover and replica promotion change the serving database. Reconnect, refresh DNS appropriately and validate the application rather than assuming existing sessions survive.

remember: Availability replication and read scaling are different jobs.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: A Multi-AZ DB cluster is different from a classic standby

sections.heading: Name the deployment
sections.text: The PDF's non-readable standby describes the classic Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. It does not describe every current RDS Multi-AZ architecture.

sections.heading: Use cluster readers
sections.text: Supported Multi-AZ DB clusters have a writer and two readable instances in three AZs. Check engine, Region, instance and feature compatibility.

sections.heading: Keep the distinction useful
sections.text: Choose the deployment from availability, read scale, failover behavior and cost. A similarly named feature is not evidence of identical replication semantics.

remember: State the deployment type before describing its readers.

title: Replica routing balances connections, not identical query loads

sections.heading: Select eligible readers
sections.text: Send read-only work to healthy replicas that satisfy the application's tolerated lag. Keep writes and read-after-write requirements on a suitable path.

sections.heading: Understand weighted DNS
sections.text: Weighted records influence DNS answers. Resolver caching, client connection pools and long-lived sessions prevent an exact per-query traffic split.

sections.heading: Monitor the result
sections.text: Compare replica lag, connection counts and query load. Health checks for private endpoints need a supported monitoring signal rather than direct public probes.

remember: Equal DNS weights do not guarantee equal database work.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: RDS encryption and auditing protect different layers

sections.heading: Protect stored data
sections.text: KMS encryption covers supported storage and snapshots. Oracle and SQL Server TDE is a separate engine feature with edition and configuration requirements.

sections.heading: Protect the session
sections.text: Use supported TLS with certificate verification. An encrypted snapshot copy can support migration from an unencrypted source snapshot; plan a tested restore.

sections.heading: Observe the right activity
sections.text: CloudTrail records supported service API actions, not every SQL statement. Enable suitable engine audit or query logs and secure their destinations.

remember: A control-plane audit trail is not a SQL audit log.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: IAM database authentication supplies a short-lived login token

sections.heading: Prepare both identities
sections.text: Supported RDS MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL configurations can use IAM database authentication. Configure the database user and the caller's rds-db:connect permission.

sections.heading: Connect with TLS
sections.text: Generate a token for the intended endpoint, port and database user. It is valid for 15 minutes for authentication; use the supported TLS connection path.

sections.heading: Retain SQL grants
sections.text: IAM authentication does not replace database authorization. Token expiry does not itself terminate an already established database session.

remember: A login token identifies a connection; database grants govern its SQL.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Oracle recovery depends on the destination platform

sections.heading: Restore to managed RDS
sections.text: Use supported RDS backup and restore workflows for RDS for Oracle. Managed access differs from a self-managed Oracle host.

sections.heading: Export supported RMAN backups
sections.text: RDS administrative packages can produce supported RMAN backups. Transfer eligible files through S3 for recovery to a compatible self-managed Oracle host; RMAN cannot directly restore an RDS instance.

sections.heading: Check engine constraints
sections.text: RDS for Oracle does not support Oracle RAC. TDE and DMS have their own prerequisites; using Oracle on EC2 transfers more operating responsibility to you.

remember: Match the backup format to a supported restore destination.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: A MySQL migration needs a consistent seed and controlled cutover

sections.heading: Create a consistent export
sections.text: A supported mysqldump workflow can seed a compatible external MySQL target. Preserve schema objects, character sets and an appropriate consistency strategy.

sections.heading: Catch up the target
sections.text: Where supported, configure replication from the correct binary-log position or GTID state. Monitor errors and lag; a completed file import is not a completed migration.

sections.heading: Cut over deliberately
sections.text: Quiesce writes, verify synchronization and target behavior, then switch the application. Stop or retire replication only after validation and a defined rollback decision.

remember: Export, catch up and cut over are separate phases.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: RDS Proxy pools connections through a private endpoint

sections.heading: Reduce connection pressure
sections.text: Bursty application clients can exhaust database connections. RDS Proxy manages a reusable pool, subject to database capacity and configured limits.

sections.heading: Build the private path
sections.text: The proxy is not publicly accessible. Place it in the database VPC with required subnets, security groups and a reachable client path.

sections.heading: Keep application discipline
sections.text: Use supported IAM or secret-based authentication. Transaction state and session pinning can reduce multiplexing; the proxy does not fix slow SQL or unlimited concurrency.

remember: A connection pool reduces overhead; it does not create database capacity.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Proxy read-only endpoints target eligible Aurora readers

sections.heading: Separate read and write paths
sections.text: Use the appropriate proxy endpoint for writer traffic. An additional supported read-only endpoint sends connections to Aurora reader instances.

sections.heading: Prepare actual readers
sections.text: A read-only endpoint needs eligible healthy replicas. Verify permissions, topology and supported engine configuration; an endpoint name does not create a replica.

sections.heading: Observe pool behavior
sections.text: Connection reuse, pinning and reader lag affect the workload. The proxy's read-only routing is different from attaching an RDS proxy directly to an ordinary RDS read replica.

remember: Choose a supported proxy target and the correct endpoint role.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Cross-Region RDS recovery requires promotion and application cutover

sections.heading: Replicate before failure
sections.text: An eligible cross-Region read replica receives asynchronous changes. Track lag and accept that the latest committed source data may not be present during an outage.

sections.heading: Detect and decide
sections.text: Use an application health route or supported metric/alarm signal to drive a controlled recovery workflow. Avoid promoting solely because one transient probe failed.

sections.heading: Recover the serving path
sections.text: Promote the intended replica, validate data and permissions, then update the application's endpoint or DNS. Fence the old writer and plan later reconciliation.

remember: Detection, promotion and cutover together determine recovery time.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora separates database compute from distributed storage

sections.heading: Choose compatible SQL
sections.text: Aurora offers MySQL-compatible and PostgreSQL-compatible engines. Compatibility does not mean every upstream feature or operational behavior is identical.

sections.heading: Share a cluster volume
sections.text: Database instances use distributed storage replicated across three AZs. Storage growth and reader compute scaling are separate mechanisms.

sections.heading: Use current limits
sections.text: Maximum storage depends on engine version; the PDF's 128 TB figure is not a universal current ceiling. Compare eligible 128 TiB and 256 TiB configurations explicitly.

remember: Separate compute scaling from storage capacity.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora storage replication is different from reader replication

sections.heading: Protect storage across AZs
sections.text: Aurora maintains six storage copies across three AZs, with self-healing distributed storage. The storage system is separate from application-facing reader instances.

sections.heading: Understand quorum concepts
sections.text: The classic architecture uses four-of-six write and three-of-six read quorum concepts. These describe storage durability operations, not a rule for counting SQL reader nodes.

sections.heading: Prepare compute failover
sections.text: Eligible Aurora replicas provide promotion targets. Failover duration depends on detection, topology and client recovery; an older sub-30-second figure is not an application guarantee.

remember: Six storage copies do not mean six SQL database instances.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora endpoints select different connection destinations

sections.heading: Writer and reader
sections.text: The cluster writer endpoint follows the current primary. The reader endpoint distributes connections among eligible readers, rather than load-balancing each SQL statement.

sections.heading: Custom subsets
sections.text: A custom endpoint represents a chosen group of instances. Use it when a workload needs a particular subset, while retaining other endpoints where appropriate.

sections.heading: Instance diagnostics
sections.text: An instance endpoint addresses one specific instance. Useful for diagnosis, it does not automatically follow a different promoted instance.

remember: Choose an endpoint by its routing behavior, not its label alone.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Custom endpoints isolate a deliberate reader workload

sections.heading: Create a useful subset
sections.text: Group compatible larger replicas for analytical queries or another defined workload. Check membership and custom-endpoint type as the topology changes.

sections.heading: Route the application
sections.text: Configure the analytical connection pool to use that custom endpoint. Ordinary reads can continue to use the reader endpoint; creating a custom endpoint does not retire it.

sections.heading: Validate isolation
sections.text: Measure CPU, waits and lag on the selected readers. A connection-routing subset does not guarantee complete resource or storage isolation.

remember: Custom endpoints express routing intent; verify the actual workload.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora reader scaling follows demand within configured bounds

sections.heading: Scale reader compute
sections.text: Supported Aurora Auto Scaling changes the number of replicas from configured targets and minimum/maximum bounds. Storage auto-expansion is independent.

sections.heading: Allow time to respond
sections.text: Creating and warming readers takes time. Persistent connections can remain on existing instances; a new reader does not instantly rebalance all sessions.

sections.heading: Keep write capacity visible
sections.text: More readers do not directly increase a single writer's write capacity. Measure writer load and route only suitable read traffic away.

remember: Scale the constrained layer and test the response time.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora logs reveal different kinds of database activity

sections.heading: Choose the engine signal
sections.text: Aurora MySQL can expose error, slow-query, general and supported audit logs. Aurora PostgreSQL has different logging controls; do not copy parameter names blindly.

sections.heading: Collect deliberately
sections.text: Download or publish supported logs to CloudWatch Logs. Configure engine parameters, retention, access controls and encryption as required.

sections.heading: Control cost and sensitivity
sections.text: Verbose query logs can increase cost and reveal sensitive SQL values. Enable the evidence required for diagnosis or audit and verify that records arrive.

remember: Select logs by the question and the database engine.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Diagnose database load before resizing the instance

sections.heading: Start with waits and SQL
sections.text: Use current CloudWatch Database Insights capabilities to inspect database load, waits and high-impact SQL. Correlate the time window with the user-visible symptom.

sections.heading: Compare system evidence
sections.text: CloudWatch metrics show resource trends. Enhanced Monitoring adds supported operating-system and process detail; slow-query logs reveal expensive statements.

sections.heading: Resolve the cause
sections.text: CPU pressure, lock waits, storage latency and connection exhaustion require different fixes. The older Performance Insights console workflow has changed; preserve the diagnostic method.

remember: A slow database needs evidence before a larger instance.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity within your chosen range

sections.heading: Choose a capacity envelope
sections.text: Serverless v2 adjusts supported database-instance capacity in Aurora Capacity Units within configured bounds. Engine version, Region and workload compatibility still matter.

sections.heading: Plan for variable demand
sections.text: Intermittent or unpredictable work can benefit from elastic capacity. Test warm-up, connection management and the minimum capacity required by the application.

sections.heading: Price the whole service
sections.text: Supported auto-pause to zero depends on engine/version and settings. Storage, I/O and other charges may remain; serverless is not automatically the cheapest option.

remember: Automatic scaling still needs limits, compatibility checks and cost modeling.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: The Data API runs SQL over HTTPS with explicit permissions

sections.heading: Use the service interface
sections.text: Supported Aurora configurations expose the RDS Data API so clients can execute SQL through HTTPS without managing a persistent database socket.

sections.heading: Authorize the request
sections.text: Grant the required Data API and Secrets Manager access, plus applicable KMS permissions. Database credentials and SQL privileges still exist behind the interface.

sections.heading: Match the workload
sections.text: Check engine/Region support, response-size and transaction constraints. Current Data API support extends beyond the PDF's older Serverless-only description.

remember: Removing a client socket does not remove authentication or SQL authorization.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Aurora Global Database separates regional reads from the writer

sections.heading: Use the primary Region
sections.text: One primary Region owns the writer. Secondary clusters serve local read workloads using asynchronously replicated storage changes.

sections.heading: Plan the current topology
sections.text: Current supported configurations allow up to ten secondary Regions, with constraints on primary readers and secondary clusters. Do not reuse the PDF's older five-Region limit.

sections.heading: Measure recovery
sections.text: Planned switchover and unplanned failover have different data-loss conditions. Monitor lag, validate eligible versions and rehearse application reconnection.

remember: Regional replicas reduce read latency; regional recovery remains a procedure.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Write forwarding still commits changes in the primary Region

sections.heading: Enter through a secondary
sections.text: Supported global write forwarding allows an application on a secondary cluster to submit eligible write statements without managing a separate writer connection.

sections.heading: Forward to the writer
sections.text: The primary cluster performs the change first, then replication propagates it. This is not an independent multi-writer database in every Region.

sections.heading: Choose consistency behavior
sections.text: Supported session/read consistency settings affect when secondary reads observe forwarded changes. Cross-Region latency and statement restrictions still apply.

remember: A local endpoint does not make the write local.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Move to Aurora through a supported migration path

sections.heading: Check source compatibility
sections.text: Eligible RDS engines and versions can migrate using supported snapshot restore or Aurora replica workflows. Validate extensions, parameters and application SQL.

sections.heading: Seed and synchronize
sections.text: A snapshot path creates a new target from a recovery point. A supported replica path can reduce the final catch-up window before promotion.

sections.heading: Validate the cutover
sections.text: Compare data, performance, security and connection settings. Switch applications deliberately and retain the agreed rollback source until validation is complete.

remember: A new engine endpoint is not proof of a completed migration.

title: DynamoDB items use a fixed key and flexible attributes

sections.heading: Define the table identity
sections.text: Choose the table's primary-key schema at creation. Each item needs the required key attributes; non-key attributes can vary between items.

sections.heading: Use supported values
sections.text: Scalar values include strings, numbers, binary, Boolean and Null. Lists and maps hold documents; supported set types hold unique scalar values.

sections.heading: Respect item limits
sections.text: An item is limited to 400 KB including attribute names and values. Managed storage growth does not make individual items or request capacity unlimited.

remember: Flexible attributes do not remove a deliberate key design.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Partition and sort keys encode the access pattern

sections.heading: Distribute partition values
sections.text: A partition-key-only table requires a unique key per item. Choose a diverse workload key rather than concentrating all requests on one hot value.

sections.heading: Group related items
sections.text: A composite key uses partition key plus sort key; their combination is unique. Items sharing a partition key can be queried in sort-key order.

sections.heading: Work an example
sections.text: Use USER#42 with GAME#101 and GAME#102 for one user's games. Time-oriented sort keys can support ranges when their encoding preserves the required order.

remember: A good key makes the important query direct.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Query and Scan do different amounts of work

sections.heading: Query a known partition
sections.text: A Query uses partition-key equality on a table or index, with an optional supported sort-key condition. Model access patterns around those keys.

sections.heading: Treat filters correctly
sections.text: A filter removes results after items are read. It does not turn a broad read into a cheap key lookup or remove the capacity already consumed.

sections.heading: Control scans and pagination
sections.text: A Scan reads across the target; large results require pagination. Parallel scans increase throughput demand and can compete with production traffic.

remember: Returning fewer rows does not prove fewer items were read.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: LSIs and GSIs create different alternate access paths

sections.heading: Local secondary index
sections.text: An LSI retains the table partition key and changes the sort key. It must be created with the table and shares table capacity.

sections.heading: Global secondary index
sections.text: A GSI can use a different partition key and optional sort key. It can be added later, with its own index capacity behavior and eventual read consistency.

sections.heading: Plan projected data
sections.text: Choose projected attributes, uniqueness assumptions and storage/write cost. Indexes support specified queries rather than unrestricted relational search.

remember: Choose an index from the query and its consistency needs.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: DynamoDB capacity mode changes billing and scaling behavior

sections.heading: Provision planned capacity
sections.text: Provisioned mode uses read and write capacity units, with optional Auto Scaling within bounds. Scaling response and hot-key distribution still matter.

sections.heading: Use on-demand deliberately
sections.text: On-demand mode bills for requests and adapts capacity under documented limits. Sudden growth, per-partition limits and configured maxima still need testing.

sections.heading: Size actual operations
sections.text: Read size, consistency and transactional operations affect consumed capacity; writes are rounded by item size. Compare measured demand rather than only request count.

remember: A capacity mode is not a promise of unlimited instantaneous throughput.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Choose read consistency for the result the user needs

sections.heading: Eventually consistent reads
sections.text: A read can briefly return an older committed version. This is often acceptable for catalogs or feeds and has different capacity cost.

sections.heading: Strong reads in supported paths
sections.text: Strongly consistent reads are available on supported table and LSI operations. GSIs and Streams do not offer strong reads.

sections.heading: Separate global semantics
sections.text: A strong read in an eventually replicated global table does not guarantee the latest write from every Region. Current multi-Region strong consistency is a distinct mode.

remember: State both the read path and the replication mode.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Transactions and conditional writes protect different invariants

sections.heading: Use a condition for a guard
sections.text: A supported conditional write can prevent overwriting an unexpected version or consuming an already-used token. Retry logic must handle failed conditions deliberately.

sections.heading: Group transactional operations
sections.text: Transactions can coordinate supported items across tables in one account and Region. Limits, conflict handling and extra capacity cost apply.

sections.heading: Keep regional scope clear
sections.text: Regional transaction atomicity does not make asynchronous global replication transactional across Regions. Multi-Region strong global tables have separate feature restrictions.

remember: Choose the smallest operation that protects the business invariant.

title: TTL expiration is asynchronous cleanup, not an exact scheduler

sections.heading: Store the expiry correctly
sections.text: Use the configured TTL attribute with a numeric Unix epoch value in seconds. An application's date string is not the same representation.

sections.heading: Expect delayed deletion
sections.text: Expired items can remain until DynamoDB removes them. Filter or reject stale records in the application when expiry affects correctness.

sections.heading: Observe downstream effects
sections.text: TTL removals can appear in Streams; replicated deletes and backup retention have separate behavior. TTL is not an authorization boundary or a scheduled job guarantee.

remember: Enforce business expiry even while the item still exists.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: DynamoDB Streams exposes ordered changes per item

sections.heading: Choose the record view
sections.text: Configure keys-only, new image, old image or both images as required. Stream records are retained for 24 hours.

sections.heading: Build a resilient consumer
sections.text: Supported Lambda or custom consumers process changes. Preserve idempotency, retries, partial-failure handling and monitoring.

sections.heading: Keep ordering scoped
sections.text: Changes for one item preserve their sequence; there is no universal order across every table item. A stream is change capture, not the database's permanent backup.

remember: Process each change safely even if the consumer retries.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Kinesis capture extends the DynamoDB change-processing design

sections.heading: Choose the capture path
sections.text: DynamoDB can publish item-level changes to Kinesis Data Streams. This differs from consuming the native 24-hour DynamoDB Stream.

sections.heading: Set retention and consumers
sections.text: Kinesis supports configurable retention beyond 24 hours. Account for delivery duplication, ordering considerations and consumer checkpoint/replay behavior.

sections.heading: Connect processing and delivery
sections.text: Use supported Lambda, Managed Service for Apache Flink or Data Firehose integrations to transform and deliver records to destinations such as S3, Redshift or OpenSearch.

remember: Longer retention helps replay only when consumers handle records correctly.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Eventually consistent global tables support regional local writes

sections.heading: Replicate between Regions
sections.text: Multi-Region eventual consistency global tables accept supported writes in replica Regions and asynchronously propagate changes.

sections.heading: Understand conflict behavior
sections.text: Concurrent updates need a deliberate conflict-aware application design. Regional transactions and strong local reads do not remove replication delay.

sections.heading: Separate routing and caching
sections.text: Route clients to a healthy Region and monitor replication. Cross-Region writes bypass another Region's DAX cache, so cached values can remain stale until refresh.

remember: Active regional writes still need conflict, lag and cache planning.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Strong global tables use a different replication contract

sections.heading: Choose MRSC explicitly
sections.text: Current multi-Region strong consistency synchronously replicates a write to another Region before successful completion. It is distinct from the PDF's asynchronous model.

sections.heading: Design the quorum topology
sections.text: Supported MRSC uses exactly three Regions: three replicas, or two replicas plus a witness. A witness cannot serve application reads or writes.

sections.heading: Review feature trade-offs
sections.text: Region combinations, latency, transactions and TTL support have mode-specific constraints. Test the selected topology rather than treating MRSC as a checkbox on every existing table.

remember: Global strong consistency changes latency, topology and supported features.

title: DynamoDB table classes and backups answer different cost questions

sections.heading: Choose the table class
sections.text: Standard and Standard-IA trade request and storage costs differently. Standard-IA remains an online table class; it is not a cold archive requiring restoration.

sections.heading: Preserve recovery points
sections.text: On-demand backups and point-in-time recovery protect against logical damage. Restoration creates a new table; recreate and validate required integrations and application routing.

sections.heading: Protect the full design
sections.text: Check keys, indexes, encryption, IAM, TTL and stream configuration after recovery. Multi-Region replication is not a substitute for historical recovery.

remember: A lower storage rate and a recoverable table are separate decisions.
generationMethod: image_gen; original educational artwork; reviewed corrected variants where needed

title: Index object metadata so the application can query it

sections.heading: Capture object changes
sections.text: S3 notifications can invoke processing that records supported object metadata in DynamoDB. Handle duplicate and out-of-order events safely.

sections.heading: Design queryable keys
sections.text: Model customer/date or other access keys and indexes for object lists and date ranges. Store the S3 object reference and required metadata, not oversized payloads.

sections.heading: Maintain derived values
sections.text: A customer's total storage needs a maintained aggregate or a deliberate computation path. A metadata table does not calculate correct totals automatically.

remember: An index stays useful only if its update and reconciliation paths are correct.

title: DAX accelerates supported DynamoDB reads inside a Region

sections.heading: Cache the hot read path
sections.text: DynamoDB Accelerator serves eligible cached reads and queries with very low latency. It does not remove write-capacity bottlenecks or every hot-partition problem.

sections.heading: Use the DAX client
sections.text: Applications use a supported DAX-aware client and endpoint. Supported writes through DAX reach DynamoDB and update relevant item-cache behavior.

sections.heading: Operate the cluster
sections.text: Deploy privately with suitable IAM, encryption and monitoring. Production designs typically use at least three nodes across AZs; node count and cache settings remain explicit.

remember: DAX is specialized caching with its own client and availability design.

title: DAX item and query caches have different freshness behavior

sections.heading: Select the read path
sections.text: Strongly consistent reads pass through DAX to DynamoDB rather than being satisfied from the cache. Cached reads use eventual consistency.

sections.heading: Understand two caches
sections.text: An item-cache entry and a cached Query/Scan result are separate. A write-through item update does not automatically repair every previously cached query result.

sections.heading: Plan expiry and bypasses
sections.text: Default TTL is five minutes unless configured otherwise. Writes that bypass DAX, including global-table replication, can leave cached results stale until expiration or refresh.

remember: A cache hit is fast; verify whether its freshness is acceptable.

title: DAX and ElastiCache serve different cache contracts

sections.heading: Choose DynamoDB-aware caching
sections.text: DAX understands supported DynamoDB item and query operations through its client. It is useful when those access patterns dominate.

sections.heading: Choose application-managed caching
sections.text: ElastiCache can hold aggregates, rendered results, sessions and other application-defined values. The application owns serialization, keys and refresh logic.

sections.heading: Account for the work
sections.text: Neither choice removes IAM, network, capacity or failure planning. A computed aggregate in a cache needs a correct invalidation or rebuild path.

remember: Match the cache interface to the value and query being accelerated.

title: Cache-aside makes the miss path part of the architecture

sections.heading: Read the cache first
sections.text: The application looks up a stable cache key. A valid hit can avoid a database read and reduce latency.

sections.heading: Fill on a miss
sections.text: On a miss, read the authoritative database, then store an appropriate value with an expiry policy. The application still returns the database result.

sections.heading: Keep the database protected
sections.text: Concurrent misses can cause a stampede. Use suitable request coalescing, bounded retries, jitter or other controls and monitor hit rate and database load.

remember: A cache that misses safely is more useful than one with a pretty hit path.

title: Cache invalidation connects writes to future reads

sections.heading: Choose a write strategy
sections.text: A database update can invalidate a cached value or refresh it through an application-controlled write path. Define the ordering and failure behavior.

sections.heading: Use TTL as a bound
sections.text: Expiration limits how long some stale data may remain, but cannot guarantee immediate correctness after every write. Sensitive workflows may need source reads.

sections.heading: Handle races
sections.text: A slow reader can refill old data after an invalidation. Versioned keys, conditional updates or suitable coordination can prevent stale resurrection.

remember: Cache correctness depends on ordering as well as expiry.

title: A shared session store helps application instances stay replaceable

sections.heading: Write session state centrally
sections.text: After authentication, store the required session state with a suitable identifier and expiry. Keep credentials and tokens protected.

sections.heading: Read from any instance
sections.text: Another application instance retrieves the same authorized session. Load-balancer stickiness is no longer the only way to reach that state.

sections.heading: Plan loss and expiry
sections.text: Cache eviction, failover or expiration can end sessions. Define acceptable reauthentication behavior and secure transport, access and cookie settings.

remember: Stateless application servers still depend on state somewhere.

title: Compare cache engines and deployment models separately

sections.heading: Valkey or Redis OSS
sections.text: Supported deployments provide rich data structures, replication, snapshots and failover capabilities. Verify the exact engine/version and operating mode.

sections.heading: Node-based Memcached
sections.text: Traditional Memcached nodes shard disposable data and use a multithreaded engine. They do not inherit Redis replication or snapshot behavior.

sections.heading: Current serverless differences
sections.text: Serverless Memcached supports snapshots, so the PDF's blanket no-backup statement is too broad. Managed ElastiCache also should not be described as providing generic Redis AOF durability.

remember: Engine family and deployment model both change the feature set.

title: Replication, sharding and persistence solve different cache risks

sections.heading: Shard for capacity
sections.text: Distribute keys across shards to spread memory and request load. Hot keys and uneven key distribution can still constrain a shard.

sections.heading: Replicate for availability
sections.text: Supported Valkey/Redis deployments use replicas and Multi-AZ automatic failover. Reader traffic may see replication lag.

sections.heading: Recover deliberate state
sections.text: Snapshots and tested restore procedures protect eligible cache data. Replication is not a backup, and persistence support depends on the selected deployment.

remember: Availability, scale and recovery need separate evidence.

title: Find the limiting layer during an extreme-rate event

sections.heading: Trace the complete request
sections.text: Edge caches, API throttles, compute concurrency, connection pools, database partitions and encryption APIs can each constrain the path.

sections.heading: Measure demand units
sections.text: Requests per second, concurrent work, I/O size and cache hit rate are different quantities. A fast cache does not fix an overloaded write path.

sections.heading: Use current quotas
sections.text: The PDF's combined rate chart contains historical defaults and simplifications. Confirm Region/account quotas, burst behavior and service-specific limits instead of treating any layer as unlimited.

remember: The smallest effective capacity on the actual path sets the limit.

title: OpenSearch is a search index with a chosen operating model

sections.heading: Choose the search use case
sections.text: Full-text search, log analytics, clickstream exploration and security analysis benefit from indexed documents and suitable mappings.

sections.heading: Select managed or serverless
sections.text: Managed domains expose cluster capacity choices. Serverless collections use a different capacity and security model; confirm workload and feature support.

sections.heading: Keep a durable authority
sections.text: An indexed copy can lag behind its source. Plan reindexing, retention, availability and recovery rather than assuming the search engine replaces every transactional database.

remember: Search freshness and transactional correctness are different promises.

title: Ingestion, search and dashboards are separate components

sections.heading: Ingest and transform
sections.text: Supported Logstash or managed ingestion pipelines collect and transform events. Protect credentials, buffer failures and monitor rejected records.

sections.heading: Index the documents
sections.text: Mappings, shard design and lifecycle settings affect search behavior, scale and storage cost. Validate document shape before indexing at volume.

sections.heading: Explore the results
sections.text: OpenSearch Dashboards queries indexed data for visual analysis. It does not itself replace every log collector or define the source's retention policy.

remember: A dashboard is only as complete as the data pipeline behind it.

title: A DynamoDB search index is an asynchronously maintained view

sections.heading: Keep transactional operations on DynamoDB
sections.text: Use the table's API for authoritative item reads and writes. Search uses a separate OpenSearch endpoint.

sections.heading: Process changes into documents
sections.text: The PDF's Streams-to-Lambda pattern can maintain the index. Handle retries, deletes, duplicate delivery and event ordering or document versioning.

sections.heading: Build a repair path
sections.text: Monitor lag and failed indexing. Backfill or reindex from a trusted source after gaps; current managed integration options also need their own compatibility checks.

remember: A successful database write is not proof the search index is current.

title: Choose a CloudWatch Logs delivery path by latency and operations

sections.heading: Use a supported subscription
sections.text: A subscription filter can deliver matching log events through a supported Lambda-based OpenSearch integration. Permissions, retries and destination capacity matter.

sections.heading: Buffer through Firehose
sections.text: A supported Data Firehose path buffers delivery into OpenSearch. Buffer settings trade latency for throughput and request behavior.

sections.heading: Verify both paths
sections.text: Do not describe either route as zero-latency or loss-proof. Monitor delivery errors, rejected documents, retry limits and recovery storage.

remember: Choose the pipeline from measured latency and failure requirements.

title: DocumentDB compatibility requires application validation

sections.heading: Use the document model
sections.text: DocumentDB supports selected MongoDB-compatible APIs for JSON-like documents, queries and indexes. It is not the MongoDB engine itself.

sections.heading: Understand the deployment
sections.text: Supported instance-based clusters use a primary, replicas and distributed storage across three AZs. Other deployment types have different limits and behavior.

sections.heading: Test real compatibility
sections.text: Validate drivers, operators, indexes, transactions and failover with the actual application. A compatibility label is not proof that every MongoDB feature works.

remember: Test the application's API usage before committing to a migration.

title: DocumentDB cost depends on storage configuration and workload

sections.heading: Account for compute and storage
sections.text: Instance-based deployments charge for database instances and stored data. Reader replicas add compute cost even when storage is shared.

sections.heading: Compare I/O models
sections.text: Standard and supported I/O-Optimized configurations have different pricing structures. The PDF's separate per-I/O model is not universal across current configurations.

sections.heading: Include recovery and traffic
sections.text: Backup storage, data transfer and workload growth affect total cost. Benchmark representative reads/writes and verify current Region-specific pricing.

remember: Compare the complete bill for a measured workload.

title: Time-series databases organize values around time and dimensions

sections.heading: Model the observations
sections.text: Use timestamps, dimensions and measures for IoT or operational metrics. Multi-measure records and time-aware queries can reduce repetitive application logic.

sections.heading: Understand historical LiveAnalytics
sections.text: Its design combines recent memory storage with historical magnetic storage, SQL, scheduled queries and time-series functions, with encryption in transit and at rest.

sections.heading: Check current eligibility
sections.text: Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers on 20 June 2025. Evaluate the current Timestream for InfluxDB options separately; do not assume identical APIs or tiering.

remember: Preserve the time-series concept while choosing an available product.

title: A time-series pipeline needs validated producers and consumers

sections.heading: Ingest supported records
sections.text: IoT applications, Kinesis, Lambda or supported stream-processing components can transform events into the selected time-series service's write format.

sections.heading: Control event time
sections.text: Handle late arrivals, retries, duplicates and retention. Producer throughput does not prove successful persistence or query readiness.

sections.heading: Expose useful analysis
sections.text: Use supported SQL/JDBC, dashboard or machine-learning integrations for the chosen product. The PDF's LiveAnalytics integrations do not automatically apply to InfluxDB.

remember: Validate each integration against the selected time-series engine.

title: DynamoDB walkthrough: prove a key query and index query

sections.heading: Create an illustrative table
sections.text: In a sandbox, create a table with PK and SK. Write USER#42/GAME#101 and USER#42/GAME#102 items with different result values.

sections.heading: Verify the access path
sections.text: Query PK=USER#42 and a supported SK condition. Compare it with a Scan and inspect consumed capacity and pagination behavior.

sections.heading: Test an alternate key
sections.text: Create an appropriate GSI for the alternate access pattern, wait for it to become active and query it. Expect eventual consistency and clean up sandbox resources.

remember: A successful query demonstrates the key design better than a table screenshot.

title: RDS recovery walkthrough: restore before changing production DNS

sections.heading: Inspect the recovery point
sections.text: In a sandbox, confirm a usable snapshot or latest restorable time, the engine/version and the required KMS key permissions.

sections.heading: Restore and validate
sections.text: Create a new private database with the intended subnet/security settings. Connect using authorized credentials and verify representative records and application operations.

sections.heading: Rehearse cutover
sections.text: Update only the sandbox application's endpoint, reconnect and measure recovery time. Retain a clear rollback decision and remove test resources afterwards.

remember: A restore test ends with usable data and a working client.

title: Proxy walkthrough: test pooling under a controlled burst

sections.heading: Prepare the sandbox path
sections.text: Create a supported proxy for the intended database. Configure private reachability, security groups and the selected authentication method.

sections.heading: Compare connection behavior
sections.text: Send a bounded test workload through the proxy and compare client connections with database connections. Inspect borrow latency, capacity and session pinning.

sections.heading: Validate failure and cleanup
sections.text: Test a denied principal or blocked path deliberately, then restore the configuration. Close clients and remove temporary resources after collecting the evidence.

remember: Verify pooling and failure behavior with observed metrics.

title: Cache walkthrough: demonstrate a hit, stale value and refresh

sections.heading: Observe the first read
sections.text: Use a sandbox application with a database and cache. Start with a missing cache key; confirm the source read and cache fill.

sections.heading: Make freshness visible
sections.text: Read again to demonstrate a hit, then change the source value. Observe the selected invalidation or TTL behavior rather than claiming instant refresh.

sections.heading: Verify recovery
sections.text: Remove or expire the cache value and prove the application returns the correct source result. Test a controlled cache outage, then clean up the sandbox.

remember: A cache demo must prove correctness as well as speed.

title: Aurora imports and exports S3 data through engine-specific features

sections.heading: Choose the engine operation
sections.text: Supported Aurora MySQL configurations use LOAD DATA FROM S3 and SELECT INTO OUTFILE S3. Aurora PostgreSQL uses supported aws_s3 extension functions instead.

sections.heading: Prepare both permission layers
sections.text: Grant the cluster the required S3 and applicable KMS permissions and network path. The database user also needs the engine-specific SQL privilege or role.

sections.heading: Validate the data movement
sections.text: Check format, engine/version, Region and account restrictions. A data export is not a complete transactional database backup; verify the intended import or query result.

remember: A common S3 destination does not make the two engines' commands interchangeable.

title: RDS event notifications complement metrics and query evidence

sections.heading: Subscribe to useful events
sections.text: An RDS event subscription selects supported resources and categories such as backup, failover or configuration changes, using an SNS topic for notifications.

sections.heading: Prepare reliable consumers
sections.text: Confirm required subscriptions and permissions. Notifications can be delayed and are not guaranteed to arrive in event order; design automation around verified resource state.

sections.heading: Correlate the symptom
sections.text: An operational event is different from CPU metrics, database waits and SQL audit records. Combine the signals that answer the question before taking a recovery action.

remember: An event message is a signal to investigate, not proof that recovery is complete.
